Among the public buildings of a certain town, which for several good reasons I had better leave unnamed, without even giving it an invented name, stands an institution once familiar in towns of every size: a workhouse. In that workhouse, on a date I need not bother to specify, since it cannot possibly matter to the reader at this point in the proceedings, the small mortal named at the head of this chapter was born.

For some time after the parish surgeon introduced him into this world of grief and difficulty, it remained seriously doubtful whether the baby would live long enough to receive any name. Had he failed to do so, these memoirs would almost certainly never have appeared. Or, if they had, their entire contents would have occupied a couple of pages, giving them the priceless distinction of being the shortest and most accurate biography in the literature of any country or age.

I do not intend to argue that birth in a workhouse is, in itself, the luckiest and most enviable event that could befall a human being. I do maintain, however, that in this particular case it was the best thing that could possibly have happened to Oliver Twist. The difficulty was persuading Oliver to undertake the business of breathing, an inconvenient practice that habit has made essential to comfortable existence. For a while he lay gasping on a small mattress stuffed with scraps of wool, suspended rather unevenly between this world and the next, with the balance decidedly favouring the next. Had attentive grandmothers, anxious aunts, experienced nurses, and profoundly learned doctors surrounded him during those moments, they would unquestionably have killed him in very short order. As it happened, the only people present were an elderly pauper woman made somewhat hazy by an unusually generous supply of beer, and a parish surgeon who handled such matters under contract. Oliver and Nature were therefore left to settle the question between themselves. After a few struggles, Oliver drew breath, sneezed, and announced to the workhouse residents that the parish had acquired a fresh burden. His announcement took the form of a cry as loud as could reasonably be expected from a male infant who had possessed that useful accessory, a voice, for little more than three minutes and fifteen seconds.

But I can ask you two questions, can't I?"

"You can ask," Monks said, looking slightly surprised. "Whether I answer is another question."

"That makes three," Mr. Bumble remarked, attempting a joke.

"Is that what you expected me to give you?" the matron demanded.

"Yes," Monks replied. "What's the other question?"

"What will you do with it? Can anyone use it against me?"

"Never," Monks answered. "Or against me either. Look here! But don't take a step forward, or you won't live to regret it."

He suddenly swung the table aside, seized an iron ring in the floor, and lifted a large trapdoor. It opened so close to Mr. Bumble's feet that he hurried several steps backward.

"Look down," Monks said, lowering the lantern into the opening. "Don't be afraid of me. If I'd wanted to, I could easily have dropped you through while you were sitting over it."

With this encouragement, the matron moved to the edge. Even Mr. Bumble, driven by curiosity, ventured closer. Muddy water, swollen by the heavy rain, rushed below them. Its splashing and swirling against the green, slimy support posts drowned every other sound. A watermill had once stood underneath. The current foamed around its remaining rotten stakes and broken machinery, then seemed to rush faster once free of these obstacles that could not hold it back.

"If you dropped a man's body in there, where would it be tomorrow morning?" Monks asked, swinging the lantern through the dark opening.

"Twelve miles downriver, and torn to pieces too," Bumble answered, shrinking back at the thought.

Monks pulled the small package from inside his coat, where he had hurriedly hidden it. On the floor lay a lead weight that had once belonged to a pulley. He tied the package to it and dropped it into the water. It fell perfectly straight, broke the surface with a barely audible splash, and disappeared.

The three looked at each other and seemed to breathe more easily.

"There!" Monks said, letting the trapdoor fall heavily shut. "If the sea ever gives up its dead, as the books say it will, it'll keep its gold and silver—and that rubbish with them. We've nothing more to discuss. Our pleasant gathering can end."

"Certainly," Mr. Bumble said eagerly.

"You'll keep your mouth shut, won't you?" Monks asked, giving him a threatening look.

In my own country and time, this money came from import duties, and the citizen comforted himself with the notion that foreign importers footed the bill. In reality the American people paid it, divided so precisely and impartially among them that the yearly charge to a man worth a hundred million and to a labourer's nursing infant was identical: six dollars apiece. I doubt anything could be more equal. Scotland and Ireland paid tribute to Arthur, and the combined inhabitants of the British Isles numbered somewhat fewer than a million. A skilled workman's average earnings were three cents daily when he provided his own board. On that basis, the national administration cost ninety thousand dollars annually, roughly two hundred and fifty each day. By handing out nickels instead of gold on a royal healing day, therefore, I harmed nobody, disappointed nobody, satisfied everyone, and additionally saved four-fifths of the day's national expenditure. In the America of my time, that would have represented eight hundred thousand dollars. For this reform I had consulted a distant store of wisdom: my childhood. A genuine statesman rejects no wisdom merely because its source is humble. As a boy I invariably kept my pennies and donated buttons to the foreign missions. Buttons served the ignorant savage as well as money, while money suited me better than buttons; everybody was content and no one suffered.

Marinel dealt with the patients in order. He inspected each applicant and turned away anyone who failed to qualify; the acceptable ones went forward to the king. A priest recited, 'They will lay hands upon the sick, who will recover.' The king then stroked the sores as the reading proceeded. At the end the patient passed the course, received his nickel—hung round his neck by the king in person—and departed. Would you suppose such a procedure effective? It certainly was. Any ceremonial nonsense will cure when the patient's belief is powerful enough. Near Astolat stood a chapel marking the place where the Virgin had appeared to a goose-herding girl, according to the girl's own testimony. A picture of the event hung inside. You would have thought that picture unsafe for an invalid to approach; instead, thousands of sick and crippled people prayed before it each year and left in perfect health. Even healthy visitors could look at it and survive.
